analysis.one_liner: Excludes all stock dividends from individuals' federal taxable income.
analysis.headline: The dividend-tax repeal died in committee: referred to Ways and Means on January 7, 2003, it drew zero cosponsors and never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove dividend income from every individual's taxable income, ending the "double tax" in which corporations pay tax on their profits and shareholders pay tax again on the dividends those profits fund. It was a one-page bill that went to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and was never considered.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that receive stock dividends — a group concentrated among wealthier households and retirees with large portfolios — would pay no federal income tax on that income at all. Publicly traded companies would also gain, since untaxed dividends make stock a cheaper way to raise money.

how_it_helps.text: Would strike dividends from gross income for individuals, so a shareholder's dividend check would face no federal income tax at all, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2002.

Would end the second layer of federal tax on corporate profits: companies already pay tax on their earnings, and shareholders currently pay again on the dividends distributed from those after-tax earnings.
Savers who live partly on dividend income, including retirees with stock portfolios, would keep the full amount of each dividend instead of paying income tax on it.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose all income tax collected on individual dividends, and everyone else would absorb that shortfall through more debt or offsetting taxes and cuts. Wage income would stay fully taxed, leaving workers with no equivalent break.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury and ordinary wage earners

drawbacks.text: The bill removes dividend income from federal taxation entirely; because dividend income flows disproportionately to households with large stock portfolios, the tax savings would concentrate at the top while the lost revenue is shared by everyone through borrowing or offsetting taxes.
It would create a stark preference for investment income over work: a dollar of dividends would go untaxed while a dollar of wages is taxed at full ordinary rates.

The drafters had to add special conforming rules so the exclusion could not be used to inflate Earned Income Tax Credit eligibility or shield Social Security benefits from tax — a sign of how the exclusion could be worked around, and of the bookkeeping the change would require throughout the tax code.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: ending double taxation of dividends is a coherent policy goal, and some middle-income retirees with dividend portfolios would keep meaningful money. But the cost is broad and the gains are top-heavy — dividends skew heavily to the wealthiest households, so this is a large revenue giveaway to them, with no offsets, paid for by everyone else through debt or other taxes. A well-designed version would pair the exclusion with a way to replace the lost revenue; this one-page bill did not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Collins introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, the opening day of the 108th Congress.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the panel that writes tax law, that same day.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.
The bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and general taxpayers kept dividend income on the tax rolls, avoiding a revenue loss that would have flowed mainly to the wealthiest shareholders; no shareholder gained anything because no tax change ever took effect.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote was ever taken, and the bill's only backer was its Republican sponsor — it drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Would exempt all individual dividend income from federal tax, a benefit that concentrates on households with the largest stock portfolios. The offsetting revenue loss falls on taxpayers generally.
Untaxed dividends would make stock more attractive to investors, lowering the cost of raising capital. That gain comes at the price of federal revenue everyone else must cover.

Ordinary dividends paid to fund and REIT investors would become tax-free, but the bill deliberately carves out capital-gain dividends from regulated investment companies and REITs, which stay taxed under existing rules.

industries.industry: Farm cooperatives and employee stock ownership plans
industries.note: Dividends from Section 521 farmers' cooperatives and Section 404(k) ESOP dividends are specifically excluded from the new tax break, apparently because those distributions already receive favorable treatment elsewhere in the code.
